parameters.content:
## Register

`POST /webhook/auth/register`
`{ "email": "a@b.com", "password": "...", "name": "Vansh" }`

Creates the account **unverified**, then emails a 6-digit code AND a one-click link -- either confirms it.

Re-registering an unverified address is allowed and just sends a fresh code, so a lost email is never a dead end. An already-verified address is refused with 409.

## Confirm the code

`POST /webhook/auth/verify`
`{ "email": "a@b.com", "code": "123456" }`

Wrong codes increment a counter and the token dies after 5 tries, so a 6-digit code cannot be brute-forced. Success consumes the token immediately.

## Resend the code

`POST /webhook/auth/resend`  `{ "email": "a@b.com" }`

One message per **60 seconds** per address. Answers identically whether or not the account exists, so it cannot be used to discover who is registered.

parameters.content:
## Sign in

`POST /webhook/auth/login`  `{ "email": ..., "password": ... }`

Wrong email and wrong password give the **same** reply, so the endpoint never confirms which addresses exist. 8 consecutive failures lock the account for 15 minutes.

This returns only a verdict, not a session token — your app issues its own session.

nodes.notes: clears the counter on success, raises it on failure

parameters.content:
## Forgot password

`POST /webhook/auth/forgot`  `{ "email": "a@b.com" }`

**Always** answers 200 with the same sentence, whether or not the address exists. Any difference — wording, status code, even timing — turns this into a way to test which emails are registered.

The link is single-use and expires in 30 minutes.

## Set the new password

`POST /webhook/auth/reset`
`{ "email": ..., "token": ..., "password": "new one" }`

Consumes the token, re-hashes with a **new** salt, clears any login lock, and emails a notice that the password changed — which is how a victim finds out if someone else did it.

parameters.content:
## Before this goes live

**1. `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN=crypto`** must stay on the n8n container. Remove it and every chain here fails closed — nobody can register or sign in.

**2. Add these MongoDB indexes** (one time):
```
db.auth_users.createIndex({email:1},{unique:true})
db.auth_tokens.createIndex({email:1,kind:1})
db.auth_tokens.createIndex({expires_at:1},
  {expireAfterSeconds:86400})
```
The TTL index sweeps spent tokens automatically.

**3. Put these endpoints behind HTTPS only** (Traefik already does) and rate limit at the edge. n8n limits per address, not per attacker.

**4. This returns a verdict, not a session.** Your app must issue its own cookie or JWT after `/auth/login` answers ok.

## Mail for the website

`POST /webhook/auth/notify`  header `x-auth-key: <secret>`
`{ "kind": "reset"|"invite", "to": ..., "url": ..., "name": ... }`

The VisionCoders site has **no SMTP of its own** and its `/forgot` and `/invitations` routes were returning the token in the HTTP response, which is an account-takeover hole. This gives it a way to post a link and have us deliver it.

**Deliberately not a general mail relay.** The caller supplies only a kind and a URL; the wording is written here, and the URL must start with the configured site origin. A leaked key can therefore only send our own two emails, pointing at our own site, never arbitrary HTML to arbitrary people.

## Sign in with a code

`POST /webhook/auth/otp-start`  `{ "phone": "9876543210" }`
`POST /webhook/auth/otp-login`  `{ "phone": ..., "code": "123456" }`

Either identifier works, and the code goes to **both** the email and the mobile on the account, so whichever arrives first is the one they type.

No password anywhere in this path. `otp-start` always answers the same way, so it cannot be used to discover who is registered.
